lead: Fenfluramine is an amphetamine-derived serotonin-releasing drug. Introduced in France in 1963 and approved in the United States in 1973 as an appetite suppressant (brand name Pondimin), it was widely used for weight loss, often with phentermine in the combination known as fen-phen.[1][2] People used it to eat less and lose body fat, which in turn changes how a person looks; roughly 5 million Americans received fenfluramine or the related dexfenfluramine from 1996 to 1998, with or without phentermine.[1]

It was withdrawn from the US market in 1997 after reports of heart valve disease and pulmonary hypertension in users.[1][5] Fenfluramine was reintroduced at lower doses as Fintepla, approved by the FDA in June 2020 for seizures in Dravet syndrome and later Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, under a restricted program with echocardiogram monitoring.[1][4][2]
Today the drug appears in appearance communities mainly as a historical diet drug, discussed in older T Nation threads about prescription fat-loss agents.[25][26]

angle.text: Fenfluramine was prescribed as a short-term appetite suppressant for obesity, so that people eating less would lose weight. It is no longer marketed for weight loss; its only current approval is for seizure disorders.

infobox: Rx-only (US, EU); removed from US Schedule IV in December 2022[1]

paras: Fenfluramine was prescribed for short-term obesity treatment. Wikipedia reports that about 5 million people in the US received fenfluramine or the related dexfenfluramine in 1996 to 1998, with or without phentermine, and that roughly 50 million Europeans were treated for appetite suppression between 1963 and 1996.[1] The fen-phen combination was proposed in 1984 and was not FDA-approved as a combination.[1][5]

Grokipedia describes clinical trials showing average weight reductions of several kilograms over 12 to 24 weeks compared with placebo in people also following calorie restriction, and describes widespread off-label long-term use in the 1980s and 1990s.[2] Fenfluramine was described as an evening appetite suppressant that does not cause the jittery feeling of stimulant diet drugs in a 2009 T Nation thread, where a poster asked whether others had tried it.[25]

The current US label lists treatment of seizures associated with Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in patients aged 2 and older.[4] Consensus and review articles describe it as one of the maintenance options for Dravet syndrome alongside other antiseizure drugs.[13][20]

A 1997 report described valvular heart disease in patients who took fenfluramine with phentermine.[5] A study of appetite suppressants found an increased risk of primary pulmonary hypertension.[6] Wikipedia reports that a study of 5,743 former users found valve damage continued after the drug was stopped, and notes a roughly sevenfold increase in the chance of needing valve surgery among former users.[1] Reviews have also discussed a higher rate of valvulopathy among women.[19]

Laboratory work linked the valve findings to activation of 5-HT2B receptors, which are abundant in cardiac valves.[7][8][1] The current label carries a boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, with echocardiograms required before, during and after treatment and distribution through a restricted program.[4] Other labeled effects include decreased appetite and weight, somnolence, suicidal behavior and ideation, serotonin syndrome and increased blood pressure.[4]

Fenfluramine releases serotonin, and its metabolite norfenfluramine acts at serotonin 5-HT2 receptors.[4][1] Wikipedia also lists a lesser norepinephrine-releasing effect through norfenfluramine and activity at the sigma-1 receptor.[1] Animal work reported that it activates central melanocortin pathways, which may contribute to appetite suppression.[9] The label states that the mechanism of its seizure benefit is unknown.[4]

Fenfluramine was developed in the early 1960s and introduced in France in 1963, and approved in the US in 1973.[1] French researchers linked it to primary pulmonary hypertension in the early 1990s, and the 1996 International Primary Pulmonary Hypertension Study reported an increased risk with appetite-suppressant drugs.[1][6] The 1997 New England Journal of Medicine report of valvular disease in fen-phen users preceded the US withdrawal later that year, and other markets followed; India banned it in 1998.[5][1]

Fenfluramine was later developed for epilepsy at lower doses, leading to FDA approval in June 2020, a CHMP positive opinion on 15 October 2020 and EU approval in December 2020; the LGS indication followed in 2022.[1][2] It was removed from Schedule IV of the US Controlled Substances Act in December 2022.[1]

Fenfluramine was withdrawn in 1997 and later in other markets; India banned it in 1998.[1] In looksmaxxing and weight-loss discussions it appears mainly as a historical drug and a reference point in conversations about appetite suppressants. An early-2000 T Nation post asked for a daily Pondimin amount for weight loss, and a 2009 thread on prescription-strength fat-loss drugs mentioned it.[26][25]

Dravet syndrome: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in The Lancet in 2019 tested fenfluramine hydrochloride for seizures; a second trial in patients receiving stiripentol-inclusive regimens was published in JAMA Neurology in 2020; and a third randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in patients aged 2 to 18 not receiving stiripentol, with at least 6 convulsive seizures during baseline, was published in Epilepsia in 2023.[17][16][15] The FDA approval was based on studies enrolling 202 subjects aged 2 to 18 that showed significantly greater reductions in convulsive seizure frequency than placebo, within 3 to 4 weeks, per Wikipedia.[1] Grokipedia cites median reductions of 70.0% (0.7 mg/kg/day) and 59.5% (0.4 mg/kg/day) versus 2.4% and 9.3% with placebo in the two pivotal studies.[2]

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: a multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial conducted from November 2017 to October 2019 ran 20 weeks and was published in JAMA Neurology in 2022.[14]
Long-term: a 2025 Epilepsia paper reports long-term safety and effectiveness in children and adults with Dravet syndrome.[18]

Registered trials include studies in infants aged 1 to under 2 years with Dravet syndrome (25 participants, completed), adults with Dravet syndrome (7, terminated), CDKL5 deficiency disorder (87 participants), infantile spasms, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Rett syndrome (200 participants, recruiting) and a trial on cognition (56 participants, completed).[21][22][10][23][24][11][12] No recent trials of fenfluramine for appearance-related weight loss were found; the historical obesity evidence is described in the original approval-era studies and the harms reports above.

timeline.event: Introduced in France as an appetite suppressant.[1]
International study reports increased pulmonary hypertension risk with appetite suppressants.[6]
Withdrawn from US market after valvulopathy reports.[1][5]
Fintepla approved for Dravet syndrome in the US (June) and EU (December).[1]
Lennox-Gastaut indication added; removed from US Schedule IV in December.[1][2]

name: Fenfluramine

card.summary: Former prescription diet drug withdrawn in 1997 over heart valve harm; now a restricted epilepsy medicine.
card.note: Boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension.

quick.overview:
Fenfluramine was a widely prescribed appetite suppressant, best known in the fen-phen combination, until it was withdrawn from the US market in 1997 after reports of heart valve disease.

A low-dose form is now sold as Fintepla for certain childhood epilepsies, not for weight loss.
quick.mechanism: It releases serotonin and acts at 5-HT2 receptors, which reduces appetite; how it prevents seizures is not known.
quick.risks: The label carries a boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, and use requires echocardiogram monitoring through a restricted program.
